lesson.title: Naming the Shapes: An Introduction to Design Patterns
lesson.summary: A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a problem that shows up again and again in software design, a shared vocabulary and a tested blueprint rather than code to copy and paste.
lesson.body:
Once you can build classes, combine objects with composition, and share behavior with inheritance, you start noticing something: the same design problems keep showing up in different programs. A class that should only ever have one instance in the whole running program. A family of related objects that all need to support the same set of operations even though they behave differently underneath. A system that needs to build different kinds of objects without the rest of the program knowing exactly which one it got. Programmers ran into these same shapes over and over, in completely unrelated projects, and eventually started giving the shapes names.

A design pattern is one of those names. It is a general, reusable solution to a problem that recurs in software design, described in a way that is independent of any single program. A pattern is not a chunk of code you copy and paste. It is more like a blueprint or a strategy: an idea about how to arrange classes and objects that you adapt to your own situation. The value is twofold. First, patterns give programmers a shared vocabulary. If you tell a teammate "just make it a Singleton," they immediately understand the shape of the solution without you re-explaining it from scratch. Second, patterns capture solutions that have already been tried, refined, and debugged by a huge number of programmers, so you are not reinventing a shaky version of something that was already solved well.

One of the simplest and most famous patterns is called Singleton. The problem it solves is this: sometimes you want a guarantee that a class has exactly one instance, shared by every part of the program, instead of many separate objects that could drift out of sync with each other. A good example is an application's configuration settings. If different parts of a program each created their own configuration object, one part might change a setting that the others never see. A Singleton fixes this by controlling how instances are created: the class itself keeps track of whether an instance already exists, and if one does, it hands that same object back instead of building a new one.

```python
class AppConfig:
    _instance = None

    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._instance is None:
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
            cls._instance.settings = {}
        return cls._instance

config1 = AppConfig()
config2 = AppConfig()

config1.settings["theme"] = "dark"

print(config1 is config2)
print(config2.settings)
```

The trick lives in `__new__`, the method Python calls to actually create a new object before `__init__` sets it up. The first time `AppConfig()` runs, `cls._instance` is `None`, so the class builds a real object with `super().__new__(cls)` and gives it a `settings` dictionary to hold onto, an example of composition: the AppConfig object *has a* dictionary inside it. That new object is saved as `cls._instance` and returned as `config1`. The second time `AppConfig()` runs, `cls._instance` is no longer `None`, so the class skips creating anything new and just returns the same object again as `config2`. That is why `config1 is config2` prints `True`, they are literally the same object in memory, and why changing `config1.settings` is visible through `config2.settings` too. Running the code above prints exactly this:

```python
True
{'theme': 'dark'}
```

Many patterns lean on inheritance for a different reason: they need several classes to share a common interface so the rest of the program can treat them interchangeably. Consider a Factory, another well known pattern. Instead of writing `SmallEnemy()` or `BossEnemy()` scattered throughout your game code, you write one function, something like `create_enemy(kind)`, that decides which subclass to build and hands back an object. Because every enemy class inherits from a common base class with the same methods, the rest of the program never has to know or care which exact subclass it received. The decision about which object to construct is hidden behind one simple interface.

Design patterns are not rules to follow blindly, and reaching for one when a plain function would do can add complexity you do not need. The real skill is recognizing a recurring problem when you see it and knowing that a well tested shape for it already has a name. Keep that instinct in mind as this chapter sequence moves into Python's own file handling tools: the `with` statement you are about to meet is itself Python's built in answer to a very common design problem, guaranteeing cleanup happens no matter what.
